section.title: Children, Parents, and Servants
section.sectionRationale: Paul continues the household code begun at 5:21, moving from husbands and wives to the other two pairs of the ancient household: children and parents, and slaves and masters. As with marriage, the point is not merely social order but the reordering of every relationship around the lordship of Christ. Children obey in the Lord, fathers raise their children in the discipline of the Lord, slaves serve as servants of Christ, and masters remember that they too have a Master in heaven who shows no favoritism. The gospel reaches into the most ordinary and the most fraught of human bonds.
section.thesis: In the Lord, children are to obey and honor their parents and fathers to nurture rather than provoke, while slaves are to serve wholeheartedly as servants of Christ and masters to treat them justly, because both slave and free stand before the same heavenly Master who rewards each and shows no favoritism.
section.frameNote: Two movements: children and parents, obedience honored by God's own promise and fathers charged to raise their children in the Lord; and slaves and masters, wholehearted service rendered to Christ and authority tempered by the knowledge of a common Master in heaven who has no favorites.

units.label: Children and parents
units.note: obey in the Lord, raise in the Lord

verses.text: Children, {{hupakouo|obey}} your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
"Honor your father and mother" (which is the first {{entole|commandment}} with a promise),
"that it may go well with you and that you may have a long life on the earth."
Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the {{paideia|discipline}} and instruction of the Lord.

units.label: Slaves and masters
units.note: one Master in heaven, no favoritism

verses.text: {{doulos|Slaves}}, obey your earthly masters with respect and fear and sincerity of heart, just as you would obey Christ.
And do this not only to please them while they are watching, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from your heart.
Serve with good will, as to the Lord and not to men,
because you know that the Lord will reward each one for whatever good he does, whether he is slave or free.

And masters, do the same for your slaves. Give up your use of threats, because you know that He who is both their {{kyrios|Master}} and yours is in heaven, and there is no {{prosopolempsia|favoritism}} with Him.

hupakouo.gloss: To obey, literally to listen under, to hear and heed with a readiness to comply. It is a stronger and more active word than mere submission; it is the glad heeding of one set in authority. Children are called to obey their parents in the Lord, and slaves to obey their masters as they would obey Christ. In both cases the obedience is offered within the sphere of Christ's lordship and directed ultimately to Him.

entole.gloss: A commandment, an authoritative charge or instruction. Paul cites the fifth commandment, honor your father and mother, and notes it is the first commandment carrying an attached promise. The word roots the everyday duty of a child in the abiding moral law of God given at Sinai, showing that the household order Paul teaches is not new invention but the outworking of God's long-standing will.

paideia.gloss: Training, discipline, upbringing, the whole formation of a child through instruction and correction. It is not mere punishment but the patient nurturing of a child toward maturity. Fathers are charged to bring their children up in the paideia of the Lord, a formation shaped by and aimed at Christ, the opposite of the harshness that would provoke a child to wrath.

doulos.gloss: A slave or bondservant, one wholly bound to the service of another. In the Roman world such persons had no legal standing, yet Paul addresses them directly as responsible members of the church and as servants of Christ. The same word he uses of the bondslave he uses elsewhere of himself as a servant of Christ, so that the lowest station in the household is dignified as a place of true service rendered to the Lord.

kyrios.gloss: Lord, master, one who holds authority and ownership. Paul uses the word with deliberate force: the earthly master is a kyrios, but he himself has a kyrios in heaven, the same Master over slave and free alike. The word that names the master's power over his slave also names the greater Lord to whom the master must answer, leveling the ground before God and undercutting every abuse of earthly authority.

prosopolempsia.gloss: Partiality, favoritism, literally the receiving of a face, judging by outward appearance or status rather than by truth. God shows no such partiality: He judges slave and free, master and servant, by the same measure. This divine impartiality is the ground on which Paul relativizes the master-slave relationship, for the God who owns them both plays no favorites and will reward each according to the good he has done.

basic.context: Paul keeps applying the Spirit-filled life to the home. Children are to obey and honor their parents, and Paul reminds them that the command to honor father and mother is the first with a promise attached. Fathers are not to exasperate their children but to raise them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. Then Paul turns to slaves and masters. Slaves are to serve sincerely, as though serving Christ Himself, knowing the Lord will reward them. Masters are to treat their slaves the same way and give up threats, because they share the same Master in heaven, who shows no favoritism.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage falls into two pairs, children and parents, then slaves and masters, each addressing first the one under authority and then the one in authority. Throughout, every relationship is reframed by the phrase in the Lord and by the reminder of a heavenly Master. The abiding principle is not the preservation of ancient social structures but the transformation of every relationship by accountability to Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: Children are to hupakouo, to obey, to listen under, their parents, for the fifth entole, commandment, carries a promise. Fathers are to raise them in the paideia, the discipline and formation, of the Lord. The doulos, the slave, is to serve as a servant of Christ, and the master is reminded that he too has a kyrios, a Master, in heaven, with whom there is no prosopolempsia, no favoritism.
basic.typology: The honoring of father and mother reaches back to the law of Sinai and forward to Christ, the true Son who perfectly honored His Father. The service of the bondslave, rendered as to the Lord, foreshadows the truth that all believers are servants of Christ who was Himself the servant of all, taking the form of a doulos.
basic.christ: Christ is Lord over the whole household. Children obey in Him, fathers nurture in Him, slaves serve as though serving Him, and masters answer to Him. He is the Master in heaven who has no favorites and who rewards each one for the good he does. The passage assumes that every human authority is answerable to the one Lord who took the form of a servant.
basic.god: God is the giver of the commandment to honor parents and the guarantor of its promise. He is the impartial Judge who shows no favoritism, weighing slave and free by the same measure, and the heavenly Master over every earthly master. The passage reveals a God whose justice reaches into every household and levels the proud.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5 give the fifth commandment Paul quotes. Colossians 3 gives the parallel instructions to children, fathers, slaves, and masters. Philemon shows Paul reframing a master and slave as brothers in Christ. Philippians 2 says Christ took the form of a servant, the pattern of all Christian service.
basic.oneStory: God's design for the family goes back to creation and the command at Sinai to honor father and mother. In Christ, every relationship is taken up and reordered around His lordship, and the gospel plants a seed that dignifies the lowly and humbles the powerful. The impartial Master in heaven who levels slave and free points ahead to the kingdom where the last are first and every faithful servant is rewarded.

context.literary:
Ephesians 6:1 to 9 completes the household code that began at 5:21, and it keeps the same two-sided shape as the earlier paragraph. Each pair names first the party under authority and then the party who holds it: children and fathers, slaves and masters. In each case the person with less power is addressed first, and the person with more is given the longer or sharper reminder. The structure treats every member of the household as someone who answers directly to the Lord.

The paragraph is held together by the phrases 'in the Lord', 'as to Christ' and 'as to the Lord', and by the closing mention of 'He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven'. The repeated 'Lord' in verses 1, 4, 7, 8 and 9 gives the unit a single centre. Under it stand the commands. Notice that the code opens with the people who may be least expected to be addressed in an ancient letter, children, and that both slaves and masters are told to 'do the same' for one another in verse 9, the only passage in the code with such a direct reciprocity.

The unit also forms a bridge. It comes after the long ethic of unity and love, and it leads straight into the call to stand firm against spiritual powers in 6:10 to 20. The command that closes the household code, to put aside threats because of a Master in heaven, gives a hint of the cosmic setting that is about to open. The one who rules heaven has no favourites, and the powers that Paul is about to describe have no claim on His people.
context.historical:
The Roman household, or familia, was a legal and economic unit that included the father, his wife, children and slaves, with the father holding wide legal authority. In the Greek and Roman world, honouring parents was a widely held virtue, and children were expected to obey. What is notable is that Paul addresses children directly, since the letter was meant to be read in the assembled church. Children are treated as members of the body who can hear and obey the Lord for themselves.

The instruction to fathers stands out against a culture in which a father's authority could be harsh and in which discipline of children and slaves by force was the norm. Paul tells fathers to restrain themselves and to take on the work of upbringing as a form of teaching in the Lord.

Slavery was widespread in the Roman Empire, and a large proportion of the population in a city like Ephesus were slaves, many of them in households and some in skilled or trusted roles. A slave had few legal rights and could be sold, beaten or separated from family. Some slaves were freed, and others were bought out of slavery. Christian slaves and Christian masters sat together in the same assembly. In that setting, to say that a master has a Master, and that God does not favour the free over the enslaved, was to take away the foundation of the system's claim, even though the letter does not call for an abolition in so many words. The same apostle sends the runaway Onesimus back to Philemon as 'no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, a beloved brother', Philemon 16.
context.canonical:
The command to honour father and mother comes from Exodus 20:12 and is repeated in Deuteronomy 5:16. It stands at the junction of the two tables of the Law, between duties toward God and duties toward neighbour, and the reward in the land is quoted by Paul in a form that suits Gentile readers. The command was backed with a penalty in the Law, Exodus 21:17, and was affirmed by Jesus, who rebuked those who used religious gifts to avoid supporting their parents, Mark 7:10 to 13. Proverbs is full of instruction from father to son, the model for the 'discipline and instruction' of verse 4, as in Proverbs 1:8 and 22:6. The warning to fathers has a close parallel in Colossians 3:21.

The place of the household code in the canon is also shaped by the Old Testament's teaching on slavery and the treatment of the poor. The Law limited the servitude of Israelites, Exodus 21:2 and Leviticus 25:39 to 43, remembered that Israel had been slaves in Egypt, Deuteronomy 15:15, and forbade kidnapping, Exodus 21:16. Job asked whether the God who made him also made his servant, Job 31:13 to 15, and the prophets condemned oppression, Isaiah 58:6 and Amos 2:6.

In the New Testament, Colossians 3:22 to 4:1 is the parallel, Philemon is the pastoral test case, and 1 Peter 2:18 to 25 holds up Christ's suffering as the pattern of the servant. The phrase 'no favoritism' draws on a Hebrew idea of God's impartiality found in Deuteronomy 10:17 and 2 Chronicles 19:7, and is quoted in Romans 2:11 and Colossians 3:25. Paul's argument that slave and free are alike in Christ is also in Galatians 3:28 and 1 Corinthians 12:13.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul's purpose is to show how the Spirit-filled life reaches into the most ordinary relationships. He does not conclude his instruction with a rule of the church, but with the family and the workplace, because it is there that the gospel is either believed or not. The same words, 'in the Lord', make the child's obedience, the father's patience and the slave's work all acts of worship.

He wants children to learn early that obedience has a place in God's order, and that the command to honour parents is no mere ancient rule but one backed by a promise. He wants fathers to see that their authority has a limit, and that the point of it is to bring children to the Lord, not to display power. He wants slaves, who might otherwise think their work had no meaning, to know that they serve Christ, and that He sees what no earthly master sees. And he wants masters to understand that they too are servants.

Beneath the practical teaching is the statement that gives it all weight: there is no favouritism with the Lord. In a society built on gradations of rank, Paul reminds each party that the one who is Lord of all does not look at status. The command makes ordinary work and ordinary obedience matter, and it pulls the ground away from pride.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The instructions to children and parents are plain commands and apply to every Christian household. Children obey in the Lord; fathers, and by extension parents, avoid provoking their children and give them Christian formation. These are lasting instructions, though they must be applied with wisdom to the age of the child. The command to obey is addressed to children who are under their parents' care, and the wider command to honour continues for adult children as well, as Jesus shows in Mark 7:10 to 13.

The instructions to slaves and masters need a more careful reading, since they address a social institution that Scripture records and regulates but does not endorse as good. The apostle is describing how believers should behave within a system they did not choose and could not end. It would be a serious misreading to take these verses as approval of slavery, or to use them to defend any form of forced labour. The Bible condemns slave trading, 1 Timothy 1:10, and Paul urges Philemon to receive Onesimus as a brother. What carries forward is the principle: work done honestly and wholeheartedly as for the Lord, and authority exercised without threats in the knowledge of a Master in heaven. This applies to employers and employees, and to anyone who has power over another.

Also note that the promise attached to the fifth commandment is a general principle, not a guarantee for each person. Proverbs and the book of Job both show that obedience does not always bring a long life, and Paul does not turn the promise into a formula.

debates.question: In what sense is the fifth commandment 'the first commandment with a promise'?

views.label: First in order among the Ten
views.case: The commandment about parents is the first of the Ten to carry an explicit promise of blessing attached: 'that it may go well with you and that you may have a long life'. The commandment about idols speaks of steadfast love to a thousand generations, Exodus 20:6, but that is part of the explanation of God's character, not a promise attached to obedience in the same way. The simple reading is that Paul describes the order.

views.label: First in importance for children
views.case: Others take 'first' to mean that this is the primary commandment for children, the first one a child is taught to keep, which carries a promise for the young.

views.label: The first in the second table
views.case: A third view is that Paul speaks of the first of the commandments that deal with duties to other people, where the promise stands at the head.

debates.bearing: None of the views changes the force of the command. All agree that Paul is quoting Scripture to give a reason for obedience beyond mere custom: it is the Lord's word, and it is tied to His blessing.

debates.question: What does Paul's instruction to slaves and masters imply about slavery itself?

views.label: It reflects the institution without endorsing it
views.case: Many see the apostle as writing within a social structure that could not be changed at once, and as sowing principles that undermine it: the master is a fellow servant, God has no favourites, and Philemon is told to treat a slave as a brother. Paul also condemns kidnapping and trading in people in 1 Timothy 1:10.

views.label: It reveals a limit in the apostolic ethic
views.case: Others argue that the absence of an explicit call to abolish slavery shows that the apostles did not see it as an urgent matter, and that Christians should be cautious in reading modern commitments into the text. Some defenders of slavery in the nineteenth century used these verses in that way.

views.label: It sets a trajectory that later believers followed
views.case: A third reading is that the New Testament sets a direction, in which every person is equal in Christ, and that later Christians, such as those who campaigned against the slave trade, were following that trajectory to its natural end.

debates.bearing: The text cannot be used to defend slavery, since it speaks to the conduct of believers within it and cuts at the root of its claims. The question of how far Scripture itself pushed toward abolition is debated, but nearly all agree that the principles of Ephesians 6:9 and Philemon 16 have no room for ownership of persons as property.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for 'obey' in verse 1, hypakouo, is built from 'hear' and 'under', and carries the sense of listening in a posture of submission. It is the verb of the child who answers a call. It is used of the wind and sea obeying Jesus, Mark 4:41, and of the believers who obeyed the teaching from the heart, Romans 6:17. The word for 'honour' in verse 2, timao, is broader and means to treat as weighty, and it continues beyond childhood. That is why the Law's command is quoted as 'honour', while the specific instruction to the child is 'obey'.

In quoting the fifth commandment Paul adjusts the promise slightly. In Exodus 20:12 the promise concerns the land that the LORD gives, while Paul speaks of 'life on the earth', using a word that can mean either land or earth. The change makes the promise fit a church that was not settled in Canaan, and keeps its principle: a household that honours God is stable.

The instruction to fathers uses the verb parorgizo, 'provoke to anger', where the parallel in Colossians 3:21 uses erethizo, which means to stir up or exasperate. The remedy is to 'bring up', ektrepho, which Paul used in 5:29 for the husband who nourishes his own body. The same verb describes nourishment: a father is to feed his children's souls. The 'discipline', paideia, is the word for the whole upbringing of a child, including correction, and in Hebrews 12:5 to 11 it is used of the Father's training of His sons. The 'instruction', nouthesia, is literally a 'putting in mind', a word of warning and counsel. Both are 'of the Lord', which can mean that the Lord is the source, the content or the aim of the training.

For slaves Paul chooses the word doulos, and in Philippians 2:7 Christ Himself takes the 'form of a doulos'. The phrase 'fear and trembling' in verse 5 is the same phrase Paul uses for the whole Christian attitude of reverent seriousness in Philippians 2:12. 'Sincerity', haplotes, means singleness, an undivided heart, as in Colossians 3:22 and 2 Corinthians 11:3. The word for 'eye-service' in verse 6, ophthalmodoulia, appears in the New Testament only here and in Colossians 3:22: it names the slave who works hard only when the master is watching.

The motivations are drawn from Christ. 'As to the Lord' in verse 7 repeats the preposition 'as', and 'good will', eunoia, describes a willing disposition of the heart. In verse 8 the verb komizo means to receive back, as if the Lord holds a ledger of every good deed. The final word, prosopolempsia, translated 'favoritism', is a Greek coinage built from a Hebrew phrase for 'lifting the face', that is, showing partiality to the one who is important, and it appears only in the New Testament, in Romans 2:11, Colossians 3:25, James 2:1 and here. 'Give up' threats translates a participle that means loosen or relax, as one lets go of a rope. In verse 9 the word kyrios appears for the earthly master and again for the heavenly one, so that the master's own title is turned back on him.

typology.type: The fifth commandment and the obedient Son
typology.fulfillment: The command to honour father and mother is the pattern of the child's place within God's order, Exodus 20:12. It finds its truest keeping in Jesus, who at twelve was found in His Father's house and went home to Nazareth and was obedient to His parents, Luke 2:49 to 51. The perfect Son also obeyed His Father in all things, John 8:29, and 'learned obedience' through suffering, Hebrews 5:8. Believers are brought into the family of God and share in the Son's relationship, Galatians 4:6. The type falls short because no earthly child honours perfectly, and the promise of long life is fulfilled finally in eternal life.

Isaiah describes the Servant who will bring justice, Isaiah 42:1, and who will be despised and bear the sins of many, Isaiah 53:11. Christ took up this role, taking the form of a servant, Philippians 2:7, and saying that He came not to be served but to serve, Mark 10:45. His washing of the disciples' feet, John 13:14, shows the master as servant. The slave who serves Christ shares His pattern, and the master who serves with kindness does the same. The pattern is partial since Christ is also Lord, and His service is a gift that no one can repay.

typology.type: The Master in heaven and the day of reckoning
typology.fulfillment: The Law and the prophets teach that the LORD is no respecter of persons, Deuteronomy 10:17, and that He judges the oppressor and lifts the downtrodden. Paul sees this fulfilled in Christ, who will judge the living and the dead, 2 Timothy 4:1, so that each person receives what is due for what has been done, 2 Corinthians 5:10. Jesus' parables of the servants who await their master's return, Luke 12:35 to 48, place the same expectation in front of every follower. The type is not complete until that day, and the present order of masters and servants is temporary.

study.christ:
Christ is named as the one in whom every relationship of the household stands. Children obey 'in the Lord', fathers raise their children in the discipline of 'the Lord', slaves serve 'as to Christ' and 'as servants of Christ', and masters answer to a Master in heaven. The word 'Lord' occurs, in one form or another, in nearly every verse. Paul places the whole domestic scene under His rule.

He is also the example. The obedient child is a picture of the Son who always did what pleased the Father, John 8:29, and of the boy who went down to Nazareth and was subject to His parents, Luke 2:51. The slave who serves wholeheartedly recalls the One who took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:7, who knelt to wash feet, John 13:5, and who gave His life as a ransom, Mark 10:45. The father who nourishes and does not provoke recalls the God who disciplines those He loves, Hebrews 12:6, with a love that is both firm and patient.

Christ is the one who rewards. 'The Lord will reward each one for whatever good he does', verse 8, is a promise that no hidden faithfulness is wasted. The slave who works unseen and unthanked is working for one who sees and repays, and Jesus Himself said that even a cup of cold water given in His name will not lose its reward, Matthew 10:42. The promise is grounded in grace, not in the idea that people earn what they receive. Paul says elsewhere that we are saved by grace, Ephesians 2:8 to 9, and that rewards are the gift of a generous Master, Matthew 20:1 to 16.

Christ is also the one who humbles the powerful. The master is told to remember that he too has a Master, and that this Master shows no favouritism. The Lord of glory who was crucified, 1 Corinthians 2:8, is the standard by which every earthly rank is measured. Jesus told His disciples that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, but that it must not be so among His followers, Mark 10:42 to 45.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The passage does not make slaves into pictures of Christ in a way that justifies slavery, and it does not claim that every child's obedience is automatically Christ-like. What it says is that the Lord is present in each relationship, and that His example reshapes the conduct of each person within it. The deepest connection is that the Son who obeyed became the one in whom all of the redeemed are adopted as children of the Father, Galatians 4:4 to 7.
study.god:
This passage reveals God as the one with whom there is no favouritism. The phrase 'no favoritism with Him' is among the most important statements about God's character in the letter, and it is stated at the very point where social difference was greatest. The Lord who is over all does not weigh slave against free or rich against poor. Moses said as much when he told Israel that the LORD their God is God of gods and Lord of lords, who shows no partiality and accepts no bribes, Deuteronomy 10:17. Paul's use of it is a reminder that God's justice is not shaped by human rank.

He is the God who gives commandments with promises. The fifth commandment is not an arbitrary rule but a gift that carries blessing with it. God cares about the order of families, and He wants children to flourish. The promise attached shows a God who delights to bless obedience and who ties the stability of a community to the way it treats the generations.

He is the Father who disciplines in love. The word for discipline in verse 4 is the same used for the Lord's own training of His children in Hebrews 12. When a human father is told to raise children in the Lord's discipline, he is being told to imitate God's way with His own family, which is neither neglectful nor harsh, but patient and purposeful. Fathers are told not to provoke, because God Himself does not exasperate His children, though He does correct them.

He is the heavenly Master who sees. The slave is told that the Lord will reward every good deed. This means that God is aware of work that no human notices, and that He values faithful service in the least regarded position. The same God is the judge of those who hold power, so that threats and cruelty are matters He will answer. Both justice and mercy are present: justice for the powerful, mercy and honour for the weak.

The presence of 'the Lord' throughout also shows the divinity of Christ. Paul uses the same title for Christ that the Greek Old Testament uses for God, and gives Him the places of Master, Rewarder and Judge. The apostle can move from 'the Lord' in verse 1 to 'God' in verse 6 without a break, since the will of God and the service of Christ are one.

For worship, the passage invites believers to see that the ordinary rhythms of home and work are places where God is honoured. A child's obedience, a parent's patience and a worker's honesty are small acts of praise, offered to the one who sees all and shows no favourites.

crossReferences.note: The fifth commandment in its original form, with the promise of long life in the land that the LORD gives. Paul quotes it, adjusting the setting for a Gentile church, and so shows that the command to honour parents is still in force.

A father's instruction and a mother's teaching are described as a garland and a chain for the child. It shows the kind of loving instruction behind Paul's 'discipline and instruction of the Lord' and supports the idea that the home is the first school of wisdom.

Paul's companion letter carries a nearly identical code, which shows these were settled apostolic teaching and not a local improvisation. Its reason for the warning to fathers, that provoked children may lose heart, and its closing appeal to masters to give what is right and fair, add detail that Ephesians leaves out.

Paul sends Onesimus back to Philemon no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother, and asks him to welcome him as he would welcome Paul. It is the clearest example of how the gospel changes the relationship of master and slave from inside.

The LORD shows no partiality, defends the fatherless and the widow, and loves the foreigner. It is the Old Testament root of Paul's 'no favoritism' and shows that God's impartiality is expressed in care for the vulnerable.
Christ takes the form of a servant and becomes obedient to death. It gives the pattern for every Christian servant and shows that the lowest position has been filled by the Lord of glory.

The boy Jesus goes down to Nazareth and is obedient to His parents, and grows in wisdom and stature. It is the living example of the command to children, and shows the Son who honours earthly parents while serving His heavenly Father.

The Lord disciplines those He loves, and discipline seems painful at the time but later yields a harvest of righteousness. The same word as in Ephesians 6:4 is used, and it shows the model that fathers are to follow.

There is neither slave nor free, for all are one in Christ Jesus. It states the principle behind Ephesians 6:8 and 9 and helps to explain why Paul places master and slave in the same assembly under the same Lord.
Paul lists among the lawless those who traffic in people. It shows that the apostle condemned the trade in human beings, and keeps the household code from being read as a defence of slavery.

study.oneStory:
The household code takes us back to the beginning, where God sets men and women in families and tells them to fill the earth. The family is the first human community, and the Bible keeps returning to it. Cain and Abel are brothers, Abraham is called to be the father of a nation, and the Passover is celebrated household by household. The command to honour father and mother stands at the centre of the Law because the passing on of faith from one generation to the next was how God planned to preserve His people, Deuteronomy 6:6 to 7 and Psalm 78:5 to 7.

Slavery is also woven into the story. Israel's founding event is an escape from slavery in Egypt, and the Law uses that memory to teach compassion, Deuteronomy 15:15. The prophets denounce those who oppress the poor. When Paul writes, the Roman Empire is built on slave labour, and the church has to find its way as a community where slave and free sit together. The story does not end with Ephesians 6, but this passage plants seeds that will grow. The Master of masters has taken the form of a servant, and the order of the world is being turned.

Paul's final remark that there is no favouritism with the Lord has a long Old Testament background and a long future. The God who brought slaves out of Egypt shows no partiality, and the one who sits on the throne in Revelation is worshipped by people from every tribe and language, Revelation 7:9. The principle moves from a statement about God to a description of the new people He is gathering.

Between the fall and the new creation, family and work are marked by pain: the child may rebel, the father may be harsh, the worker may be exploited, and the master may abuse his power. The household code does not remove all these things, but it shows how a redeemed community lives within them, with Christ as the centre. The Spirit-filled life described in the letter does not wait for a better world to begin; it starts at the dining table and the workplace.

In the end the creation will be set free from its bondage, Romans 8:21, and the faithful servants will hear the words, 'Well done', and enter their Master's joy, Matthew 25:21. The children of God will have the whole inheritance, and the Master who serves will seat them at His table, Luke 12:37. The household of God will be complete.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say the command to honor father and mother is notable?

options.text: It is the first commandment with a promise attached, that it may go well and life be long.
options.note: Verses 2 and 3 highlight the promise joined to the fifth commandment.

options.text: It is the only commandment that still applies to Christians.
options.note: Paul singles out its attached promise, not that it is the sole surviving command.

options.text: It was a new rule Paul invented for the church.
options.note: Paul quotes the ancient fifth commandment from the law, not a new invention.

options.text: It applies only to adult children, never young ones.
options.note: Paul addresses children directly to obey and honor their parents.

quiz.q: What are fathers charged to do and not to do in verse 4?

options.text: Not to provoke their children to wrath, but to raise them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
options.note: Fathers are to nurture, not exasperate, forming their children in the Lord.

options.text: To rule their children by fear so they never step out of line.
options.note: Paul warns against provoking to wrath; the aim is godly nurture, not intimidation.

options.text: To leave all instruction to others and stay uninvolved.
options.note: Fathers are actively charged to bring their children up in the Lord.

options.text: To punish every fault as harshly as possible.
options.note: Harshness that provokes children to wrath is exactly what Paul forbids.

quiz.q: How are slaves told to serve their earthly masters?

options.text: Sincerely from the heart, as servants of Christ doing the will of God, not merely to be seen.
options.note: Verses 5 to 7 call for wholehearted service rendered as to the Lord.

options.text: Only when the master is watching, to avoid punishment.
options.note: Paul says the opposite, not to please them only while they watch but as servants of Christ.

options.text: Grudgingly, since the work has no meaning.
options.note: They are to serve with good will, as to the Lord, because He will reward the good they do.

options.text: By refusing to work until they are freed.
options.note: Paul calls for faithful service within the situation, done as unto Christ.

quiz.q: What does Paul remind masters of in verse 9?

options.text: That they share one Master in heaven with their slaves, and there is no favoritism with Him.
options.note: The master answers to the same impartial heavenly Lord as his slave.

options.text: That their authority over slaves is absolute and unquestioned.
options.note: Paul limits their authority, telling them to give up threats and remember their own Master.

options.text: That God favors masters over slaves.
options.note: Paul says exactly the opposite, there is no favoritism with God.

options.text: That they owe their slaves nothing at all.
options.note: Masters are to do the same for their slaves and give up threats, answerable to God.

quiz.q: How does the passage relate to slavery as an institution?

options.text: It regulates and radically relativizes it, planting gospel principles that undermine it over time.
options.note: Common Master and no favoritism level slave and free and hollow out the institution's foundation.

options.text: It gives slavery God's permanent endorsement.
options.note: Paul never endorses slavery; he reorders the relationship under Christ and dignifies the slave.

options.text: It commands an immediate armed revolt against all masters.
options.note: Paul plants transforming principles rather than calling for a violent revolt that would have been crushed.

options.text: It says nothing of any relevance to how we work today.
options.note: The principles apply directly to modern work: sincere labor and just, humble authority, all done before Christ.

quiz.q: What truth grounds both the slave's service and the master's restraint?

options.text: That the Lord in heaven rewards each one for the good he does and shows no favoritism.
options.note: The impartial heavenly Master is the ground for both wholehearted service and just authority.

options.text: That earthly status determines one's worth before God.
options.note: Paul teaches the reverse: God shows no favoritism between slave and free.

options.text: That good deeds go unnoticed and unrewarded.
options.note: Paul says the Lord will reward each one for whatever good he does.

options.text: That masters answer to no one for their conduct.
options.note: Masters answer to the same Master in heaven who is over them and their slaves.

questions: Paul tells children to obey and honor their parents in the Lord. However old you are, how might you honor your father and mother in a way that reflects your reverence for Christ?
Fathers are warned not to provoke their children to wrath but to nurture them in the Lord. Where might firmness need to be tempered by patience in the way you shape those under your care?
Slaves were told to work sincerely as servants of Christ, not merely to be seen. How would treating your daily work as service rendered to the Lord change the way you do it?
Masters were told to give up threats and to remember their own Master in heaven. If you hold authority over anyone, how does knowing you answer to an impartial God shape how you use it?
God shows no favoritism, leveling slave and free before Him. How does the impartial justice of God comfort you if you feel powerless, and humble you if you hold power?

translationNotes.note: These verses quote the fifth commandment from Exodus 20:12 and Deuteronomy 5:16, honor your father and mother, with its attached promise; the straight double quotation marks preserve the citation of the Decalogue.
Discipline renders paideia, the whole training and formation of a child through instruction and correction, not mere punishment; the phrase of the Lord marks it as a Christ-shaped upbringing.
Favoritism renders prosopolempsia, literally the receiving of a face, that is, judging by status or appearance; Paul's point is that God weighs master and slave by one impartial measure.

meta.notes: BSB text for Ephesians 6:1-9 reproduced as supplied. Verses 2 and 3 quote Exodus 20:12 and Deuteronomy 5:16, kept with straight double quotes. punctuation kept clean per the style rule.
